newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dollar struggles after support gives way.
newsitem.headline: Australia dollar struggles after support gives way.

text.p: A souring in sentiment on the Australian dollar saw it drop to its lowest level since February as support proved less resilient than expected, and its failure to bounce solidly off its lows had left it looking vulnerable.
The dollar was sold down under US$0.7800 overnight, and support at US$0.7770 was broken in morning trading as the dollar sold to a low of US$0.7848, a level last seen in late February.
By 4.30 p.m. the dollar was at US$0.7760/65, down from an opening US$0.7781/86 and a Thursday close of US$0.7815/20.
"It looked a bit shaky this morning," one trader said. "The fact that it hasn't bounced, it doesn't look good."

The Australian dollar had trouble finding buyers through the morning, with U.S., European and Japanese names all seen behind the selling. However, locals and some offshore investors stepped in from around US$0.7750.

Even what would normally be considered favourable data for the dollar, retail trade and building approvals data suggesting that growth would rise moderately through 1997, was ignored by a market focusing more on narrowing interest rate differentials.
While there was buying interest around US$0.7750, the key support level for the dollar was now seen as US$0.7740, with little support seen between there and 77 cents.

While the dollar had not tested under US$0.7750 on the day, traders said the much-discussed backlog of exporter demand under US$0.7800 had failed to eventuate and this raised some questions about just how strong support was.
"I think the interesting thing tonight will be if it goes into Europe around US$0.7750," the trader said.
"I think they'll just try to push it down to see what's below there, more out of interest rather anything else, just to see if there are any stops below US$0.7750, or what is there."
Although the selling was mainly against the U.S. dollar, there was some Aussie/yen selling as well on the day.

The U.S. dollar rising one yen to 123.50 yen in Tokyo after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin brushed aside suggestions that a stronger yen was the best way to avoid a further rise in the trade surplus, the Australian dollar improved from its local open.
The dollar ended at 95.82/92 yen, up from an early 95.39/49 but still down on Thursday's closing 96.12/22.
In trade weighted terms the dollar was steady through the day at 59.7 after dropping from 60.0 on Thursday.
It was the lowest TWI close since March 3.

The bearish sentiment on the Australian dollar, and the market's focus on what the U.S. interest rate outlook was, especially ahead of the U.S. March payrolls data later today, meant local data was again ignored.

Retail sales rose 0.8 percent in February, which economists said was a strong figure as it followed a 2.7 percent rise in January. Building approvals fell 3.7 percent in February, but this was seen as a correction to January's very strong 10.4 percent rise.
Both sectors had been weak through 1996 but have been showing signs of strength through the early stages of this year.

"Today's numbers continue to point to recovery in these two areas," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said, adding the muted market reaction was because the data "did not change the consensus view of a moderate pick up in activity through the first quarter of 1997".
-- John Mair, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
